title.narrative: Scaling-up regenerative practices for the recovery and improvements of soils, biodiversity, and associated ecosystem services in the Chilean agricultural sector

description.narrative: Catalyze the transition toward a regenerative and circular model in Chile's food systems to recover and improve soils, biodiversity, and associated ecosystem services, thereby contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation in the national agricultural sector
Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.

With respect to the socioeconomic benefits that the project will bring, farmers, technicians, extensionists, advisors and public officials at the national and regional levels will be benefitting from the National Regenerative Training Program, totaling to at least 1,105 people (442 women and 663 men), who will strengthen their knowledge and capacities on the regenerative approach integrating a gender approach and cultural relevance in all training activities. Among the people trained, pilots producers including Peasant and Indigenous Family Farming , are considered beneficiaries of the training program whose exact number will be defined at the beginning of the project's implementation stage. It should be noted that the scope of the training will be expanded through continuous training and formal education actions, reaching a larger number of people who will benefit locally and nationally with improved knowledge and more information on regenerative systems. At pilot level, it is expected that all families of the pilot farms, including those belonging to Peasant and Indigenous Family Farming will benefit directly from the improvement of their production systems through implementation of regenerative practices (with specific investments contributed by the project), technical assistence and development of practical tools to support implementation and monitoring of results which will be defined in the Regenerative Action Plan (farm intervention work plans). In this regard, the expected beneficiaries in the pilots to reach at least 400 people (160 women and 240 men), including people from the family group linked to the producers of Peasant and Indigenous Family Farming identified during the formulation stage of the Prodoc. In particular, in the pilot project developed in the property that is part of the Senda Chacao community, actions will be carried out to provide permanent information and training to interested community members, in order to improve their knowledge, as well as to highlight cultural knowledge and the role of women in the community (for more information, see Annex F2). As part of the activities of each pilot, demonstrative activities and exchange of experiences will be developed, which will benefit various local stakeholders strengthen their knowledge and skills in regenerative systems. At the company level, it is expected that workers will benefit from the training and transfer of knowledge, which will contribute to improving their labor skills and future oportunities. The scaling-up strategy for each pilot (Component 3) is intended as a means to extend the benefits to the entire industry or sector, installing good production practices, with positive environmental impacts, such as reduction of soil and water pollution due to a reduction in the use of agrochemicals and waste management, efficient use of water resources, improvement in biodiversity conditions and in the provision of ecosystem services, increasing the adaptive capacity and climate resilience of the systems. Additionally, it is expected, to reduce occupational risks due to exposure to agrochemicals, improve food safety, strengthen food security and conservation of the agri-food heritage, promoting improved conditions for workers and local communities. This sectoral transformation will contribute to the long-term sustainability of production systems while generating tangible benefits for rural communities.Component 3 will also strengthen the value chains of regenerative products, by improving marketing conditions and strategic positioning of regenerative products through the valorization of regenerative attributes demanded by processors and consumers. In general, it is expected that income will be increased for producers through better prices and added value, generation of qualified rural employment, improvement in the livelihoods of small and medium producers, including Peasant and Indigenous Family Farming, and woman entrepreneurs. Specifically, consumers will gain access to evidence-based information on regenerative product attributes through reliable and accessible channels. Value chain participants will benefit from streamlined verification and certification systems for regenerative products, enabling access to higher-value markets. Small producers involved in the business model pilot will receive targeted training strengthening of local business capacities and guidance to overcome market access challenges, such as formalization, permit acquisition, and marketing strategies. Additionally, partnerships with public and private sectors will facilitate commercialization strategies, including direct sales, public procurement, and digital platforms. By updating public policy instruments (Component 1), technical assistance and investment will be strengthened through the integration of regenerative criteria with a gender and intercultural approach, which will have a positive impact on production systems and production chains. Considering the national scope of the public policy, it is expected that regenerative and sustainable agricultural producers will be benefited from the modified instruments through investment subsidies, technical assistance and capacity building. With respect to financial mechanisms (Component 2), these will expand access to financing traditionally underserved farmers, taking into account gender and intercultural conditions considering Peasant and Indigenous Family Farming. Agricultural producers and regenerative value chain actors are expected to benefit from the new portfolio of public and private financing available. With respect to the establishment of public-private linkages (Regenerative Hub), investments will be catalyzed, innovation will be promoted and workshops and trainings opportunities will be strengthened, actions that will benefits to agricultural producers and regenerative value chain actors at both the national and regional levels. These structural changes will lay the groundwork for a sustainable transformation of the sector, leading to measurable improvements in the quality of life and well-being of rural communities. In addition, all the activities developed within the framework of the toolkit for the dissemination and exchange of best practices will contribute to strengthening the capacities of different stakeholders in a cross-cutting manner in the project (Output 4.1.2).On the other hand, the knowledge and skills in regenerative production systems, good practices, sustainable management, biodiversity, soil and water management, and waste management of the people directly related to the pilots (at least 40 farms) will be strengthened, with a scope of at least 400 people, as well as all those who participate in the demonstration activities that will be developed over the 5 years of the project (Output 3.1.1). It should be noted that part of the indicators that are expected to be monitored in the pilots are related to decent employment and gender equity; therefore, feedback will be provided to the farms and companies participating in the topic, as well as in the public policy instruments that apply (Output 1.1.2).Actions focused on the development of marketing strategies (Output 3.2.2) will improve the income of producers and value chain actors, prioritizing Peasant and Indigenous Family Farming, and support the creation of decent employment opportunities and help reduce the income gap between men and women. It should be noted that the activities implemented by the project integrate the application of international labor standards and will support partnerships with local, regional and national stakeholders to build human capital by improving access to vocational and business training and strengthening stakeholder capacities. [1] In the definition applied by FAO decent rural employment refers to any activity, occupation, work, business or service performed by women and men, adults and youth, for remuneration or profit, in rural areas, that: 1) respects core labor standards as defined in ILO Conventions; 2) provides an adequate living income; 3) involves an adequate degree of job security and stability; 4) adopts basic occupational safety and health measures; 5) avoids excessive working hours and allows sufficient time for rest; 6) promotes access to technical and vocational training.
